slides.title: Linked Structures

blocks.text: A linked structure is a data structure that uses object references to create links between objects.
A linked structure is the alternative to an array-based implementation of a collection.
Recall that an object reference variable holds the address of an object, indicating where the object is stored in memory.
The object reference is sometimes called a pointer because its points to the object in memory.

slides.title: Self-Referential class

blocks.text: A class Person can have a data field next that references another object of the same Person class.
A series of Person objects would make up a linked list.
First Person object points to second Person object.
Second Person object points to third Person object, etc.

slides.title: Linked List

blocks.text: The objects stored in the list are called the nodes of the list.
For example, each node can be a Person object.
A separate reference variable, front, is needed to point to the first node in the list.
The last node in the list does not reference any object.
The next reference in the last node should be equal to null.

slides.title: Managing Linked Lists

blocks.text: No matter what a linked list stores, there are few basic techniques for managing the nodes in the list.
1. Accessing elements in the list.
2. Inserting elements into the list.
3. Removing elements from the list.

slides.raw_text:
Managing Linked Lists
❑No matter what a linked list stores, there are few basic 
techniques for managing the nodes in the list.
1. Accessing elements in the list.
2. Inserting elements into the list.
3. Removing elements from the list.

slides.title: Accessing Nodes in the List

blocks.text: We maintain a pointer to the first node in the list.
We use the next pointer to access the second node.
We continue until we reach the last node in the list.
Consider searching a list for a particular person name.
We use a reference variable current to traverse the list.
Continue until name is found or the end of list is reached.

slides.title: Inserting a Node at the Front of a List

blocks.text: To insert a node at the front of a list, first link the new node to the front node, then reassign the front pointer.
Inserting a node into the middle of a list requires more processing and will be discussed later.
Person node = new Person();
node.next = front;
front = node;

slides.title: Deleting the Front Node of a List

blocks.text: To delete the front node, reassign the front reference to point to the next node in the list.
To delete a node in the middle of the list requires more processing and will be discussed later.
Person next = front.next;
front.next = null;
front = next;

slides.title: Elements without Links

blocks.text: So far, we assumed that the list contains nodes that are self referential:
Person object points to next Person object. The flaw of this approach is that the Person class must become a node in a linked list.
However, we want a generic list of elements of any type T.
Solution: have a generic Node<T> class that forms the linked list and holds a reference to elements of any type T.

slides.title: Implementing a Stack with Links

blocks.text: Let us now implement our own version of a stack that uses a linked list to hold the elements.
The LinkedStack<T> class implements the same interface
Stack<T> and stores elements of generic type T.
A nested Node<T> class forms the list and holds a reference to the element stored.
An integer count stores how many elements are currently in the stack.

slides.title: The Node<T> class

blocks.text: Node<T> is defined as private static class nested under
LinkedStack<T> for better grouping and encapsulation.
It serves as the node containing a reference to the next node and a reference to the generic element of type T.

slides.title: The push method

blocks.text: The push(T) method creates a new node for an element of type T and links it to the top of the stack. It also increments the count of elements on the stack.

slides.title: Pushing Six Elements on the Stack

blocks.text: Since all activity on a stack happens on one end, a single reference represents the top of the stack.
count becomes 6 after pushing six elements on the stack.
